thread.title: The World's Economy Is Cooling Off (But It's Not All Bad) - Part II: China

author: The Fortune Teller
title: The World's Economy Is Cooling Off (But It's Not All Bad) - Part II: China
text:
Prologue By now, it's clear that the world's economy is cooling off. Almost everywhere one looks at - there are more and more signs of weakness.
In this series, we will touch upon each of the world's four largest economies, trying to figure out how bad (or good?) things are.
Part I in this series is focusing on the US ( SPY , DIA , QQQ , IWM ), the world's largest economy.
Part II, the one you're currently reading, is focusing on China ( MCHI , FXI ), the world's second-largest economy.
Part III will focus on Japan ( EWJ , DXJ ), the world's third-largest economy.
Part IV will focus on Germany ( EWG ), the world's fourth-largest economy.
By the way, the ranking isn't expected to change over the next few years.
Investment Thesis In spite of the past week's positive tone (overall) in the market, it's important to remember that we are:
Only a few weeks post the market entering a bear market territory. While a bear market doesn't automatically/necessarily lead to a recession - this isn't something that should be easily dismissed. Still seeing parts of the yield curve inverting, especially the up tenors up to five years. Once again, although a full inverted yield (usually measured by the 2s10s spread) is neither certain nor guaranteeing a recession - a 10-2 inversion is a very reliable indicator and, if and when we get there, investors should be very mindful of it. Keep getting mostly negative/"broken" economic data. As this article suggests, there are many areas within the world's economy (generally speaking) and China (specifically) that need to be addressed. In this article, we will touch upon all the recent red signals, but we will also present some points/areas that provide reasons to remain optimistic, or at least not totally pessimistic.
Our approach over the past year was to remain fully invested, but to shift:
From a more aggressive approach to being more defensive. Less growth, e.g. technology ( XLK ), more income, e.g. REITs ( VNQ ). Reducing risk and HY ( HYG , JNK , AWF , BKLN ), adding safety and IG ( AGG , BND , LQD , BSV ). Dumping long-duration ( TLT , SPTL , VGLT , IEF ), focus on short-to-medium duration ( BIL , SHV , SHY , VGSH , SCHO , STIP ) and relatively shorter tenors/intervals. Increasing the floating-rate exposure at the expense of fixed-rate. Employing more hedges by using pair trades, option-trading, and short selling. Such a shift, although it provides no protection against a market correction, has put us in a much better position to withstand the -20% drop stocks went through over a short period of time.
We strongly suggest for readers to keep their eyes wide-open and adhere to the most important thing when it comes to investing: Risk management.
Risk management isn't a recipe to avoid losses, but it's an ongoing process of asking yourself many "what IFs" type of questions. For example: What if there's no trade deal agreement? Are you ready for this?
The most important virtues any investor should strive for are: Patience, Discipline, Consistency, and Flexibility, or (as we like to call this) P-DCF.
As most of you probably know, DCF also stands for "Distributable Cash Flow". If we decide that the "P" stands for "Proven", we can say that adopting the P-DCF virtues may lead to a better, certainly safer, and Proven Distributable Cash Flow.
Ten Recent Signs of Weakness 1. This time is different.
China's current economic slowdown differs from previous downturns because this time Chinese consumers are taking a hit.
2. Credit bubble.
With the central bank trying to release more liquidity in order to support the local economy/markets the rise of the Chinese total debt to 300% of GDP is likely to be met in 2019.
3. This (manufacturing) boat is sinking.
China's Manufacturing PMI fell below 50 in December (to 49.4), the first time since February 2016.
Export orders fell for the 7th-month in-a-row.
The Caixin Manufacturing PMI fell to 49.7 in December, from 50.2 in November, and below the no-change consensus. New orders also fell, for first time since June 2016, suggesting that activity is unlikely to form a recovery until (at least) second half of 2019.
The last time China's Manufacturing PMI fell below 50, the Chinese government provided significant stimulus, which sends both the PMI and MSCI World Index sharply higher. Guess what? It happened again (for more details - look further down below)
4. Industrial profits fell for the first time since December 2015.
Anyone who was looking/hoping for signs of faster growth in China - they remain elusive for now.
5. Debt that is (almost) impossible to serve.
The interest payments alone on China's non-financial debt totaled about $3 trillion last year, equal to roughly 22% of the nation's GDP. At this point, China is borrowing more money just to cover the interest payments on its existing debt.
5. Consumption is faltering.
Chinese consumers are spending less due to higher costs of living and economic uncertainty, helping to drive the nation's slowdown. This is different from prior downturns in China.
6. Ghost cities.
More than 1 in 5 apartments in Chinese cities are unoccupied, according to some estimates. This is fueling angst as property values fall, since housing accounts for up to one-third of China's economic growth.
7. Stock market was particularly bad.
China practically has the world's worst stock market: $2.3 trillion was wiped out this year. Shanghai Composite has lost circa 30% in USD terms in 2018.
Bears have ravaged the most this year in China, South Korea ( EWY ), Mexico ( EWW ), Japan, and Germany.
China A-Share ETF ( ASHR ) at its lowest level since February 2016, down 37% from its January high.
8. Slower GDP growth and evident slowdown across many other gauges that measure/define the Chinese economic sentiment.
We are now talking about a pace of growth that is about half of what we've seen during 2010-2011. Even if we dismiss those years as being an "aftershock" bounce, it has been a long, steady, slide ever since.
9. Peer-to-Peer lending is a big problem of its own.
The number of Chinese peer-to-peer lenders may drop by 70% this year as the nation intensifies a crackdown on riskier forms of financing.
10. Trade war.
Last but not least, perhaps the master-architect of most everything that we've presented above.
In spite of the booming trade China seemingly winning this war, when measured by the US trade deficit, this is a Pyrrhic victory.
A trade surplus with the US, as big as it may be, can't stem the huge holes China is seeing in investments, retail sales, industrial production, and GDP growth.
Five Signs That Things Aren't That Bad After All 1. Stimulus? There you go!
We promised above that we will be back with the Chinese stimulus and it came out, as expected.
China's central bank just announced it will lower the Required Reserve Ratio ("RRR") of banks again to stimulate growth. The PBoC will cut 0.5% on January 15th and another 0.5% on January 25th.
Cutting the RRR by a full 1 percentage point will release about 1.5 trillion yuan of liquidity to the Chinese markets.
After only one reduction in 2016, and none in 2017, this will be the third time the PBoC is reducing the RRR over the past 9 months.
2. There's light even at the end of the darkest tunnel?
The "Chinese Manufacturing Tunnel" has been as dark as one could expect. However, the Caixin China Services PMI just unexpectedly rose in December, to a healthy reading of 53.9.
Another gauge - the IHS Markit China Composite Purchasing Managers Index (PMI), which is produced in conjunction with the Caixin Insight Group - rose in December (in seasonally adjusted terms) to 52.2, the highest level in five months.
3. This boat is shrinking.
The Chinese shadow lending activity - accounting for a big chunk of the credit bubble - is shrinking as well as transforming. The risky loans (it gives) are moving, slowly but surely, into the banking system.
On one hand, it may only be a shift of the risk from one hand to another. On the other hand, the assumption is that the banks can handle these loans in a better way (or at least tackle those with more support from the authorities) when they are on the balance sheet, rather "hiding" underneath.
4. Only a one off? Hopefully...
Following a negative month in November, that saw foreign investors pulling money out of Chinese bonds for the first time in almost two years, overseas investors have boosted their Chinese bond holdings by the most since June.
5. Trade talks.
All eyes are now on the China-US trade talks in Beijing, as investors are waiting for positive signs that will assist shrugging off the recent bad economic data (in both countries), as well as the very noisy warning alarm that Apple ( AAPL ) has sounded last week.
In spite of US-China trade taking place on January 7-8 in Beijing, no agreement is expected this week.
Current negotiations (between vice presidents) are mostly aimed at setting the stage for higher level talks soon, involving presidents Trump and Xi.
Trump will have an earlier opportunity to hold negotiations with Chinese vice president Qishan, when they both attend the upcoming World Economic Forum (January 22-25, 2019) annual gathering in Davos.
The Chinese yuan is strengthening against the USD recently. That is a good sign because a strengthening Chinese currency has coincided with more risk appetite in financial markets (and vice versa) in recent years.
In spite of the yuan ( CNY , CYB ) being under pressure over the past 20 months, it hasn't breached 7 (yuan for 1 US dollar), a very important level from both technical and psychological aspects.
Moreover, while the markets have been through a turmoil in Q4/2018, the USDCNY was quite stable and, as a matter of fact, managed to gain some ground ever since the markets start their journey south.
Epilogue China takes another step to add stimulus to its economy. The key question is, how much more ammunition does the nation have at this point, especially given how much its debt load has already increased in recent years?
The good news heading into 2019 is that Trump seems much more upbeat about the trade discussions with China.
The bad news is that the Chinese economy continues to slow down, more (and faster) than analysts have expected.
Let's not also forget that China has a dangerous "US dollar ( UUP ) debt addiction". With $1.2 trillion needing to be rolled over this year, the threat of a funding crunch is rising.
Chinese stocks have started 2019 the same way they ended in 2018 - down. That's just another bad sign, especially when the US markets managed to finish the first trading week of the new year on a positive accord.
China now spends more in debt service than it earns in incremental GDP, and its leaders know it.
The PBoC new round of stimulus is likely to only exacerbate, and certainly not solve the problem.
They're now drinking their very own Kool-Aid, believing they can gradually solve the problem, rather kicking the can down the road. Hence, they will not do another 2016-type stimulus, unless there's no other choice.
In addition, some say this is "fake news", as China is not (yet?) "really" stimulating. The PBoC balance sheet is roughly stable, mainly due to foreign assets continue to run down.
Their first choice should be - and is likely - to reach a trade deal, something that will give a boost not only to the capital markets but also to the Chinese economy, that is desperately looking for such a much-needed boost.
The sooner - the better.
